newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nobel laureate says E.Timorese have suffered enough.
newsitem.headline: Nobel laureate says E.Timorese have suffered enough.

text.p: Jose Ramos-Horta, the East Timorese resistance campaigner named joint winner of the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday, said he hoped the award would send a signal to Indonesia that it must quit the territory.
Speaking to Reuters from his mother's home in Sydney, Ramos-Horta, 46, also said that the prize should not have gone to him, but to jailed resistance leader Xanana Gusmao.
"I would feel much happier if instead of my name, his was selected," he said.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after the abrupt departure of its Portuguese colonisers.
It annexed the territory the following year in a move never recognised by the United Nations.
Ramos-Horta, who spends much of his time in Sydney, was on Friday named joint winner of the 1996 Peace Prize with Bishop Carlos Belo, East Timor's outspoken Roman Catholic bishop.
"I'm happy but surprised, because Bishop Belo deserves the Nobel Peace Prize but the other person who should be sharing the award with him is my leader, Xanana Gusmao," Ramos-Horta said.
"He's an outstanding man of peace and democracy, a man of courage...I have done my best, but there is nothing exceptional about it when your country is occupied," he said.

The soft-spoken Ramos-Horta said he hoped the Peace Prize would send a message to Indonesia "that the people of East Timor have suffered long enough and that there must be serious dialogue under United Nations auspices to resolve the problem".
"I am prepared, as I have said again and again, to fly to Indonesia for informal discussions," he said.

The United Nations has brokered regular meetings between the foreign ministers of Indonesia and Portugal -- which disputes Indonesia's administration of the territory -- and has also started an intra-Timorese dialogue.
But progress has been painfully slow, with the substantive issue of East Timor's future political status barely addressed.

The next meeting is due to be held in New York on December 21 but Ramos-Horta said it may never happen if United Nations Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali loses a battle for re-election at the end of this year.
"The talks have gone nowhere at all at this stage," he said.
Ramos-Horta, who left East Timor in December 1975, three days before the Indonesian invasion, lectures in diplomacy in the law faculty of the University of New South Wales in Sydney.
But the U.S.-educated lawyer spends much of his time travelling around the world, promoting the cause of the East Timorese people.
The Australian government congratulated Ramos-Horta and Bishop Belo on their award.
"We congratulate the Nobel laureates with whom we share the desire for a peaceful East Timor," a spokesman for Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer said.
